newsitem.title: SYRIA: French president visits Syria amid peace concern.
newsitem.headline: French president visits Syria amid peace concern.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac arrives on Saturday for talks with President Hafez al-Assad amid warnings that collapse of the faltering Middle East peace process could lead toward renewed war.
A senior French official said Chirac, who will also visit Israel, the Palestinian self-ruled areas, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt would urge regional leaders to keep hopes for peace alive.
He said Chirac would express concern that "if the current stalemate in the Middle East peace process continues the situation might deviate towards war."
"Chirac would tell all the leaders of the region the situation is dangerous and they must be careful not to allow it to diverge towards war," the official said.
The official also said an agreement for Syria to repay debts to France amounting to around 1.3 billion French francs ($250 million) would be signed during Chirac's visit.
Chirac met Arab and Israeli journalists in Paris on Friday ahead of his tour of the region.

The French official said Syria and France had made concessions to reach the ageement which would open the way for new investment and more French business in Syria. It will alow France's state credit agency guarantee new credits to Syria.
"The agreement is an ambitious economic step...France likes to do more business with Syria," the official said.
French economic sources said France was keen to expand trade with Syria, which stood at 3 billion French francs ($576 million) according to the 1995 figures.
The balance of trade is now in favour of Syria whose exports to France are mainly crude oil. Syria's total exports to France in 1995 reached 2 billion francs ($384 million).
Syrian imports from France, mainly heavy equipment and cars, stood at 1 billion francs ($192 million) in 1995. France was the third European exporter to Syria after Italy and Germany.
The French official said France considers Syria an important country for French diplomacy and Paris respects Syria's role in the region.
Syria has held sporadic peace negotiations with Israel since 1991 but none since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took over in June.

Syria and Arab states have condemned Netanyahu's refusal to accept the concept of trading occupied Arab lands for peace with Arabs. Syria wants Israel to return all of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in 1967.
Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara welcomed a more active French and European role in the Arab-Israeli peace talks, co-sponsored by the United States and Russia.

But Shara, quoted by the official Syrian news agency, said France's role would not be an alternative to that of the United States. Europe is not taking part in bilateral Arab-Israeli talks but participates in multilateral talks on regional cooperation.

The French official was asked if Lebanon was no longer a problem between France and Syria, the main foreign power broker in Lebanon where it has some 35,000 troops. Israel has occupied a self-declared security zone in south Lebanon since 1982.
He said France believed Lebanon must have full territorial integrity and sovereignty. He said the peace process and reconstruction would allow Lebanon to recover full independence.
